TMJ disorder is plausible given mechanical aggravation with chewing and bilateral temporal distribution, though typically less severe and not life-threatening. Chronic paroxysmal hemicrania is excluded by bilateral pain and lack of autonomic features or absolute response to indomethacin, but included due to severity and temporal location. Cluster headache is unlikely due to bilateral (not strictly unilateral) pain and absence of classic autonomic signs (e.g., lacrimation, ptosis), though rare atypical presentations exist. Migraine is considered least likely because it rarely presents de novo at high severity with strict chewing-triggered exacerbation and lacks typical associated features (photophobia, nausea, aura); the absence of prior headache history further reduces probability."}

The indomethacin question (though unanswered) is highly relevant: chronic paroxysmal hemicrania (CPH) is exquisitely indomethacin-responsive and can present with severe, side-of-head pain, though jaw-triggering is atypical; its inclusion reflects the diagnostic utility of that test. NDPH is considered because of new-onset severity and persistence, but lacks typical triggers or autonomic features. Atypical trigeminal neuralgia may cause dull, non-paroxysmal, chewing-aggravated pain in the V2/V3 distribution, but usually more localized and less global 'side-of-head' involvement. Cluster headache is unlikely: it is typically strictly unilateral, excruciating, associated with ipsilateral autonomic features (lacrimation, rhinorrhea), and not aggravated by chewing—though severity (10/10) and novelty are consistent. Confidence scores reflect prevalence, specificity of symptoms (jaw claudication = highly specific for GCA), and response patterns to targeted therapy."}
